newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dry helps cotton, sorghum, worries wheat.
newsitem.headline: Australia dry helps cotton, sorghum, worries wheat.

text.p: A very dry autumn in Australia's eastern agriculture belt has boosted the previously flood-hit cotton crop and allowed the sorghum harvest to proceed well, industry sources and analysts said on Tuesday.
But only weeks were left before it began to threaten prospects for winter wheat, they told Reuters.
The best news is for Australia's A$1.1 billion cotton crop, now about half-harvested.
"We believe up to 50 percent of the (cotton) crop may be picked," a Namoi Cotton Co-operative official said.
"The harvest is progressing very well," she said.
Yields were better than expected and the crop should exceed original estimates of 2.3-2.5 million 500-pound bales, she said.

This represents a turnaround from earlier this year, when cotton valleys in northern New South Wales (NSW) and southern Queensland were hit by floods and then buffetted by rains from cyclone Justin. This raised doubt by leading growers at the time that the crop would be more than 2.4 million bales.
"The rain has had an effect but this crop has managed to recover. We've had wonderful weather since (January and February)," the Namoi Cotton official said.
"It certainly wasn't as affected as people thought at the time," she said.
If current weather held about 80 percent of the cotton would be picked in another four weeks.

"We hope (rain) holds off for another four weeks, (but others) are looking for that winter break," she said. The typical southern NSW dry summer-wet winter "Mediterrean climate" was still expected to produce a break.

Michael Shean, crop forecaster with the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), and an official with leading Queensland grain co-operative Grainco Ltd, both said the sorghum harvest was headed directly for the Australian Bureau of Agricultural Economics (ABARE) forecast of one million tonnes.
"The crop is coming in as expected," Shean said. "Its factored in as almost in the bin."
ABARE forecast a planted area of 497,000 hectares would produce 1.06 million tonnes of sorghum in 1996/97, down from 1.56 million tonnes.
In Western Australia, wheat planting would start after May 1, if additional showers occur.
Opening showers were excellent but only set the stage for planting lupins and canola, he said.
In South Australia, Victoria and southern NSW, wheat planting was on hold until the rain break, needed by early to mid-May, he said.
The area sown to wheat in Australia this season could be affected only marginally by the difficult crop outlook in Europe and the U.S., he said.
The Grainco official said the sorghum harvest in southern Queensland was "all but complete", although it had not yet begun in central Queensland. Quality was generally good.
AWB's Shean said planting of 1997/98 wheat had barely begun, as was normal, with crops going in in the northern highlands of Queensland and some extremely early plantings in northern NSW.
February rainfall in northern NSW had produced very good sub-soil moisture, not enough to get the crop germinated but a substantial resource if good opening rain was received, he said.
"That sub-soil moisture is something they haven't been able to count on in years now," he said.
ABARE's preliminary wheat forecast was that 10.5 million ha would be sown to wheat in 1997/98 for production of 17.8 million tonnes, down from the record 23.0 million tonnes of 1996/97.
Cotton and sorghum are summer-grown crops in Australia, which are harvested in autumn, while wheat, as well as barley, are winter-grown and summer-harvested.
